en: The Sūtra of the Silver-Colored Woman, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhayaśas of India during the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavān was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove.
At the Anāthapiṇḍika Park, together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying: "Bhikṣus!..."

If there are sentient beings who can understand all the merits of giving and the karmic fruits of generosity as I know them, then at the time of eating, whether it be the first morsel or the last morsel, they should not eat of their own accord without having set aside a portion to give.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“If there are sentient beings who, as the Buddha has taught,
give away a portion of their food, they shall achieve a great fruit and retribution.”
"Whether with the first morsel of food or with the last morsel of food,
if one does not practice giving, then one should not eat it oneself.
At that time, having spoken this verse, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus, saying:
“O bhikṣus! In the distant past, beyond immeasurable kalpas, there was a royal capital where the king’s name was Padma.
In that city there was a woman named Rūpyāvatī—exquisite and peerless, endowed with perfect physical features, and possessing a most supreme and wondrous form.”
“Because that silver-colored woman had some need, she left her own home and went to another’s house.
Having entered that house, she saw within it a newly delivered woman who had given birth to a boy; he was handsome and exquisite, with a perfectly formed complexion.”
At that time, a woman who had recently given birth was holding her infant in her hands,
intending to eat it. Then, the girl Rūpyā asked her,
"Sister, what are you doing?"
He replied, "I am now extremely hungry and have no strength; not knowing what else to eat, I wish to devour my own child.
Then, the girl Rūpyā said to him:
"Sister, stop for a moment; this matter is not permissible.
Sister!
Is there truly nothing else in this house for people to eat?"
He replied: "Sister!
For a long time I have accumulated the defilements of stinginess, greed, and parsimony; therefore, at this moment, I have nothing to eat."
The girl of silver color said:
"Sister, stop for a moment; wait while I go home and fetch food for you.
She spoke again:
"Sister! My two sides now feel as though they are about to burst, my back feels as if it will split, my heart trembles with unease, and all directions have grown dark.
As soon as you step out of the house, my life shall come to an end."
Then the girl Rūpyā thought to herself:
"If I take my son away, that woman’s life will end;
if I do not take him away, she will surely devour this child."
"By what means can these two lives be saved?
He then said to her: "Sister!
"Is there a sharp knife in this room?
I have need of it now. He replied:
"Yes," she replied,
and immediately took a knife and handed it to Silā.
Silā took the knife and cut off her two breasts to give to him to eat, and spoke to him, saying:
"Drink this milk of mine, and it shall immediately cause your body, sister, to be freed from the suffering of hunger and thirst.
After she had taken and eaten it, he asked her again:
"Sister, are you satisfied?"
He replied, "I am full. The girl Rūpyā said:
"Sister, you should know now that this child was ransomed by my own flesh.
I shall leave him with you for the time being, as I must go home to fetch some food and drink."
Having spoken these words, blood flowed from his entire body as he dragged himself along the ground and departed.
When he arrived at his home, his silver-colored retinue and kinsmen saw him and all asked together: "Who did this?"
Rūpyā replied, “I did this myself.
He asked her again:
"Why is this so? Rūpyavarṇā replied,
"I have already resolved my mind to not abandon great compassion, for the sake of seeking to achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
The relatives all said, "Though one practices giving,
if the mind feels regret, that may be considered *dāna*, but it is not a *pāramitā*.
Having spoken these words, they questioned him further:
"Will you feel joy at the time of being cut?
Do not let such suffering give rise to regret or distress.
At that time, the maiden Rūpyāvatī immediately made this vow:
"I have cut off my two breasts without giving rise to a single thought of regret, and my mind was free from any other thought.
By this vow, may my two breasts be restored to their original state.
Having made this vow, her two breasts were immediately restored to their original state.
"At that time, the yakṣas and others within the city of Padmāvatī raised a great cry, saying:
'The girl of silver color has now herself surrendered her two breasts!
Hearing this, the Earth Deity likewise proclaimed it."
Having heard this, the devas in the void of space proclaimed it;
thus the sound was transmitted as far as the Brahma heavens.
At that time, Śakra, King of Devas, thought to himself:
"This is truly rare!
Out of compassion for sentient beings, this silver-colored woman has sacrificed her own two breasts.
I shall now go there to test her."
Having formed this thought, he immediately transformed his body into that of a brahmin.
Holding a golden water-pitcher and a golden bowl in his left hand, and grasping a single golden staff in his right hand, he then proceeded toward the royal capital of Padma.
Having arrived, he gradually made his way to the residence where the maiden Śilpā lived and stood outside the gate, calling out for alms.
When the maiden Śilpā heard the sound of the beggar at the gate, she immediately took a vessel, filled it with food according to the occasion, and went out to the gate.
Then the brahmin said to her, "Sister, please stop for now; I have no need for food.
The woman replied:
"Why is that? The brahmin replied, "I am Śakra."
"I have conceived a great doubt regarding you, which is why I have come here.
You must answer me according to what I ask.
The woman replied to him:
“Great Brahmin! Ask now whatever you wish.
I shall answer it, ensuring that it accords with your heart as a brahmin.”
Then the brahmin asked:
"Sister, did you truly cut off both breasts to give them to another?
She replied:
"It is indeed so,
Great Brāhmaṇa! The Brāhmaṇa said:
"Why is this so? The girl Rūpyā replied,
"It is because the mind of great compassion seeks to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
The brahmin said:
"This matter is extremely difficult.
That which is an extremely difficult matter is what is called *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
If, after having given a gift, one gives rise to a mind of regret, that is merely generosity (dāna), not a perfection (pāramitā).
When you give, do you feel joy?
"When it was being cut, did painful thoughts arise?
Śilpā replied, "Kauśika!..."

I now make this vow: because I seek the mind of omniscience, because I seek the supreme mind for all the world, and because I seek to save all sentient beings, I have cut these two breasts and truly feel no regret.
"If you do not repent, let my female body be transformed into that of a man.

When the girl Silver had made this vow, she immediately became a man. Seeing that her female body had become that of a man, his heart was filled with joy and he leaped for immeasurable delight; he then went to another place and fell asleep beneath a tree.
"At that time, King Padma suddenly passed away, and the king had no son.
It was then an exceedingly hot season.

During this time, the various ministers traveled from tree to tree, from village to village, from city to city, and from capital to capital, searching everywhere for a person endowed with the marks who should become king."
The ministers all said,
"How can we now obtain a king who rules according to the Dharma?
At that time, one of the great ministers, distressed by the heat, entered a lotus pond.
At that time, the minister saw the person beneath the tree, whose appearance was exceptionally sublime and endowed with all the marks of excellence;
though he lay sleeping and did not awaken, even as the sun moved on, the shadow of the tree did not leave him.
Then that minister snapped his fingers to awaken him.
Once he had awakened, he was led to Rājagṛha, where his hair was shaved and he was dressed in royal garments with a jeweled crown placed upon his head. The minister then spoke to him, saying:
"You shall now attend to the affairs of state."
He replied, "I truly cannot manage the affairs of state.
[The king] spoke to him again:
"Now I must attend to the affairs of state.
He replied again, "If I were to become king,
I would rule the country according to the Dharma."
"You all, if you would each fully undertake the ten paths of wholesome action,
I shall become king. They all replied,
"We, your ministers, will comply."
Immediately, they all received the ten paths of wholesome action.
Having thus exhorted sentient beings in these ten paths of wholesome action, that person governed the affairs of the kingdom and was named King Silver-Colored (Rajārūpya).
At that time, the lifespan of the people within the kingdom was seventy thousand nayutas of years.
After that king had governed the affairs of state for immeasurable hundreds and thousands of years, he finally passed away.
"At the time of death, one should speak these words:
'All things are impermanent; there must inevitably come the event of decay and destruction.
Where there is union, there must inevitably be separation; all who possess life must surely die.'"
"Whatever deeds one performs, whether virtuous or non-virtuous, for all who are born,
their lives do not endure for long.
When that king passed away, he was reborn in that very place, the royal city of Padma.
He took rebirth in the wife of the elder, and after eight or nine months, a boy was born who was handsome and exquisite, endowed with all excellent features.
When that boy reached the age of eight, five hundred boys surrounded him as they were about to go to the schoolhouse.
In that schoolhouse, there were previously five hundred boys studying scripts.
At that time, those boys asked the seniors: "What are you doing here?"
The elder replied,
"We study writing.
He spoke again:
"What benefit or profit do you gain from studying writing? Why must you study this writing?
You should simply resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*."
The elder youth asked:
"When one resolves upon the mind of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, what is it for?
The youth replied:
"One must practice the six pāramitās. What are these six?
They are the dāna-pāramitā, the śīla-pāramitā, the kṣānti-pāramitā, the vīrya-pāramitā, the dhyāna-pāramitā, and the prajñā-pāramitā."
Having heard this, he immediately said:
"I resolve to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
At that time, after the youth had caused all those people to resolve to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, he thought to himself:
"I now wish to give away these few trifling things as an offering.
I shall now practice giving for the sake of those with two feet, those with four feet, birds, beasts, deer, and the like."
Having formed this thought, he went at once to the Śītavana forest.
There, using a sharp knife, he pierced his body to draw blood, smearing it over his entire frame; he then anointed himself with oil, lay down in that grove, and cried out:
"All you bipeds and quadrupeds—deer, birds, and beasts, whether near or far—who require food, come here, I pray, and eat the flesh of my body!"
“At that time, among the flock of birds flying there, a bird named Hastin came and sat upon his forehead; he plucked out his right eye and then released it.”
He asked the bird,
"For what reason do you now pull out my right eye and then let it go?
The bird replied:
"Among all other parts of the human body, there is nothing more beautiful than the eye.
He then said to the bird:
"Even if you were to pull out my right eye and release it a thousand times, I would not give rise to a heart of resentment."
"Then those birds devoured his two eyes.
An immeasurable multitude of birds gathered in that forest and together ate all his flesh until nothing remained but white bones."
"After he has relinquished his body, he will immediately be reborn again in the capital city of Padmavati.
Taking birth there as the son of a Brahmin woman, after ten full months he will give birth to a boy who is handsome and exquisite, supreme and peerless, with a perfectly endowed complexion."
"After he had reached the age of twenty, his parents spoke to him, saying:
'Māṇava! You must now build a house.'"
Then the youth replied to his parents, saying:
"What is the purpose of building a house for me?
My mind is no longer set upon a house; I only wish to be released so that I may enter the deep mountains."
His parents immediately gave their consent.
He departed from his home and went into the mountain forest; having arrived there, he saw two brahmin sages who had long resided in that forest standing before him.
Then the māṇava went to where the two brahmin sages were and asked them,
"O Brahmanical Sages, what are you doing here in these mountain forests?"
The two sages replied:
"Māṇava! We all practice various forms of asceticism in this forest for the sake of benefiting sentient beings."
He spoke again, saying:
"I have now also come here for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, desiring to practice asceticism."
That māṇava then went to another forest grove, measured out the ground, and built a house.
By the power of the merit from his cultivation of wholesome deeds, that māṇava suddenly attained the divine eye.
Immediately, he saw from afar, not far from his dwelling place, a tigress staying there who was pregnant and about to give birth.
At that time, the māṇava, having seen this, thought to himself:
"This tigress will give birth before long; once she has given birth, she may die of hunger, or suffer extreme distress from starvation, or perhaps devour her own offspring."
Having thought this, he immediately asked those two brahmin seers:
"Who among you is able to cut off a portion of their own body to give to this tigress? They replied:
"We cannot cut our own bodies to give them as an offering.
Having said these words, another seven days passed, and the tigress then gave birth.
Once the tigress had given birth, she took her cubs in her mouth, placed them on the ground, and then went back to retrieve them.
At that time, having witnessed this event, the māṇava went to the two ṛṣis and said:
"Great Sages!
The tigress has given birth."
"If you practice asceticism for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, now is precisely the time; you may cut flesh from your own body and give it to this tigress.
Then those two brahmin seers went to the left side of the tigress and thought to themselves:
"Who could endure such a painful matter as this to practice such a great act of giving?"
"Who could cut off their own beloved flesh from their body to give to this starving tigress?
Having thought this, the tigress who had given birth immediately pursued them from afar.
Out of concern for their own lives, the two sages flew through the air and departed.
Then the māṇava spoke from afar to those two brahmin ṛṣis, saying:
"Is this the matter of your vow?
Having said this, he immediately made a solemn declaration:
"I now sacrifice my body to save this starving tigress.
By virtue of this cause and condition, I vow that my body shall surely attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Having made this vow, he found a sharp sword at that spot and offered his own body to the starving tigress.
"O Bhikṣus! Out of compassion for you, I have seen that doubt has arisen in your minds. O Bhikṣus!"
Do not give rise to divergent doubts;
do not entertain other views.
Why is this? You should know:
"At that time, in that city of Padmavati, was the woman of silver color who cut off her two breasts anyone else?
It was I myself, monks!"
Do not give rise to further doubts, and do not entertain other views.
Why is this? You should know:
"I was the daughter of King Padmavati, named Silver-Colored, at that time.
O Bhikṣus! Do not give rise to doubt; do not entertain any other view."
For what reason?
You should know this:
at that time, I was the girl named Silver-Colored (Rūpyā), who gave up her two breasts to save that child.
“O bhikṣus! Do not give rise to doubt, nor entertain any other view. Why is this?
You should know this:
as for Rāhula, could he be anyone else?
He was none other than that boy at that time.
“O bhikṣus! Do not give rise to doubt, and do not hold a different view. Why is this?
You should know this:
at that time, in that Śītavana forest within the royal city of Padmavati, was the one who sacrificed his body for the sake of the flock of birds anyone other than this person?
"I am that very person. "O bhikṣus!
Do not give rise to doubt; do not entertain other views."
Why is this? You should know that those two seer-brāhmaṇas at that time— could they have been anyone else?
"These are none other than you, O bhikṣus. "Bhikṣus!
Do not give rise to doubt; do not entertain any other view."
Why is this? You should know that I was the young brahmin Māṇava at that time.
“Monks! Therefore, I now instruct you, monks:
if monks know the merit of giving and the fruit of giving, they should eat by first offering a morsel or by offering a final morsel, and thus consume their food.”
When the Buddha had spoken these words, all those bhikṣus were greatly filled with joy.
The Sūtra of the Silver-Colored Girl.
